strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how collaborative workflows affect interactive qualitative coding. Comparing topic-model, relational, and LLM-based systems gives the study useful methodological breadth.
Separating consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and correctness is valuable. The reported results illustrate that improvements on one dimension need not imply improvements on others.

The evaluation includes substantial human involvement: 20 participants and a manual audit of 1,200 document–theme pairs, with two evaluators and tie-breaking adjudication. Reporting Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.632 provides useful transparency about judgment reliability.

The presentation is generally clear, and the appendices provide prompts, initialization settings, and interview questions. Sharing initial partitions within systems controls one source of variation. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b02/review-experiment-4ws5mxrb/call-07cf81ddeb8d45e3bbf35ca38ae029f2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Section 4 compares individual coders with three-person synchronous groups, confounding synchronicity with team size and potentially total effort. The asynchronous consolidation step described in the introduction is absent. Participant allocation, reuse, condition order, and session durations are insufficiently reported. The evidence supports an exploratory individual-versus-group comparison; stronger collaboration claims require a better-controlled design.

The statistical support is inadequate for the significance claims. Each tool has only two synchronous groups and three individual sessions, yielding just one synchronous codebook pair for consistency. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without identifying the sampling unit, sample sizes, degrees of freedom, or handling of multiple comparisons. Themes and comparisons sharing codebooks cannot automatically be treated as independent replications. Analyses must account for session and participant dependence.

The correctness evaluation is insufficiently specified and contains an interpretation discrepancy. Figure 4 reports F1 without defining its calculation or averaging, and provides no uncertainty estimates for the 200 audited pairs per condition. Treatment of invalid LLM labels is also unclear. The text claims higher topic-model correctness asynchronously, but the figure shows synchronous scores higher at the intermediate cutoffs and both conditions at approximately 0.50 for 'All'. These issues directly affect the empirical conclusions.

The proposed evaluation framework needs stronger validation. Best-theme matching does not clearly specify symmetry or one-to-one matching, and final theme counts and size distributions are absent. These properties affect maximum-overlap and embedding-similarity scores. The human audit checks document assignments, but does not establish that the automated consistency measures capture equivalent themes or meaningful improvements in codebook quality.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendices. Missing details include the exact S-BERT checkpoint, LLM decoding settings, prompt-selection sample sizes, and selected prompts for individual sessions. Final codebooks, assignments, and analysis code are promised for release but are not supplied through an identifiable artifact link.

Several explanations exceed the evidence. Interaction breadth is not independently manipulated, and the systems differ in other consequential ways, including the relational system’s use of stance and morality information. Conclusions about LLM reliability and cost rest on one Llama 3.2 3B configuration on one English tweet corpus, without comparative efficiency measurements. These observations should be scoped to the tested configurations.

The interview-based recommendations lack a sufficiently documented analysis procedure and completed-interview counts. Appendix C acknowledges missing interviews and different interview formats across conditions, which complicates comparisons of participant attitudes. Together with the design and statistical concerns, these gaps warrant revision before a sound Findings recommendation.
